subject: Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations

messages.author: 9dd9ea947d797759
messages.subject: Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
parts:
I'm working on a multivariate state-space model in which the latent process x is system of linear stochastic differential equations (two-dimensional in this case):

dx = (a + Bx(t)) dt + noise,

where a is an unknown vector and B is an unknown matrix, and the noise term (a multivariate Wiener process) has unknown covariance matrix Sigma.

There are multinomial observations at a series of time points, with parameter vector given by a one-one but nonlinear transformation of x + eta, where eta is an unknown vector. The nonlinear transformation (inverse isometric logratio) is basically the softmax of the result of multiplying x on the left by a known matrix (I didn't actually use softmax to code it, although perhaps I should have done).

It's a lot like this:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/TukPmAw84iE

apart from the nonlinear transformation and multinomial observations.

If eta is fixed, everything works fine, but when we try to estimate eta, for some simulated data sets the chains look as though they are mixing very slowly, effective sample sizes for eta and a are very small, and the R-hat for eta and a are well above 1. The posterior distributions for elements of eta are usually multimodal (because different chains do different things), and often none of the modes coincides with known values for simulated data. We also have similar but less severe problems with a when eta is estimated.

We're pretty sure that the model is identifiable (and for some simulated data sets it seems to work OK). Furthermore, similar models in which the observation process is (for example) a multivariate t-distribution with location vector given by x + eta (not transformed) work fine (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08363), which suggests to me that it's not an identifiability problem. So I think that the problem must be in how the nonlinear transformation of x + eta affects the gradient of the multinomial log-likelihood. But we don't get any warnings about Jacobian problems, and plotting log probability against the elements of eta didn't immediately suggest a funnel problem to me (although I might not have been looking in the right way).

What can I do to diagnose the problem?

I've attached a description of the model (stanusers.pdf), our current Stan code (pollen.stan), the Bash script we use to run it in cmdstan 2.12.0 (run4chains.sh) with a simulated data set (simdataBrostrom.txt), example trace plots (stansimTrace.pdf), and kernel density plots of the posterior distributions of each parameter, with the true values as red lines (plotpostparms.pdf). Pairs plots of the posterior distributions were too big too post here, but showed obvious problems with eta, and some fairly strong correlations among some other parameters. For this case, the true values used to generate simulated data in R were:

    a <- c(0.10471002, -0.03106714)
    B <- matrix(c(-0.04184048, 0.06290105, 0.01222532, -0.03466200), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
    x0 <- c(-0.7, 0.9)
    Sigma <- matrix(c(0.01, -0.005, -0.005, 0.03), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
    eta <- c(-0.69, -0.40)

and we generated 1001 equally-spaced observations, each with n = 1000 in the multinomials.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
parts:
Hi Matthew,

Thanks for being thorough. There are definitely missing pieces in the description like why the stochastic differential equation looks the way it does. (I don't know these models, so this might be obvious to people that do work on these models, bit definitely not to me.) 

Some simpler questions to start with:
Did you simulate the data from that process? 
What was the last version of this model that was fitting reliably? 

Long questions like these are hard to answer. Maybe ask your question more plainly and you'll get more help? I'll try the best I can. More below.

On Dec 11, 2016, at 10:30 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:

I'm working on a multivariate state-space model in which the latent process x is system of linear stochastic differential equations (two-dimensional in this case):

dx = (a + Bx(t)) dt + noise,

where a is an unknown vector and B is an unknown matrix, and the noise term (a multivariate Wiener process) has unknown covariance matrix Sigma.

There are multinomial observations at a series of time points, with parameter vector given by a one-one but nonlinear transformation of x + eta, where eta is an unknown vector. The nonlinear transformation (inverse isometric logratio) is basically the softmax of the result of multiplying x on the left by a known matrix (I didn't actually use softmax to code it, although perhaps I should have done).
Use softmax and run with identical seeds. Make sure results are identical. (if you're thinking it's a gradient issue, well, you should check that it's not a function value issue first.)

It's a lot like this:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/TukPmAw84iE

apart from the nonlinear transformation and multinomial observations.

If eta is fixed, everything works fine, but when we try to estimate eta, for some simulated data sets the chains look as though they are mixing very slowly, effective sample sizes for eta and a are very small, and the R-hat for eta and a are well above 1. The posterior distributions for elements of eta are usually multimodal (because different chains do different things), and often none of the modes coincides with known values for simulated data. We also have similar but less severe problems with a when eta is estimated.

The traceplots look bad. Can you show the results of fixed eta? Can you make one eta a parameter and see if that works?

Because chains end up in different places doesn't quite mean that it's multimodal. It could also mean that the posterior is improper and chains aren't actually converging. From the traceplots, it didn't look like chains were actually stuck in modes.
We're pretty sure that the model is identifiable (and for some simulated data sets it seems to work OK).

?
If you've got something to tell you that, could you enlighten me? I have intuition when things aren't identified, but I have a very hard time telling when it will be. The geometry of the unconstrained space isn't just defined by the Stan program. It's actually the joint lpdf, which depends on data. And I stay away from claims like that when it's clear that something is not correct.

Furthermore, similar models in which the observation process is (for example) a multivariate t-distribution with location vector given by x + eta (not transformed) work fine (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08363),
I didn't dig through the paper, but did you implement that model?

which suggests to me that it's not an identifiability problem.
So I think that the problem must be in how the nonlinear transformation of x + eta affects the gradient of the multinomial log-likelihood.

Or it's a non identifiability through the non linear transformation.

One thing to check: how are the values of lp__ for the different chains? If they're all roughly the same values, thats clearly a non identifiability: different values of parameters are resulting in the same joint lpdf on the unconstrained space. Quick check: traceplot the lp__.

Now, if you think it's really the gradients, there is a test gradient mode built in just for this purpose. Check the doc on your interface of choice.

But we don't get any warnings about Jacobian problems, and plotting log probability against the elements of eta didn't immediately suggest a funnel problem to me (although I might not have been looking in the right way).

Jacobian warnings are a function of the Stan program and don't have anything to do with runtime diagnosis. 

Plotting lp__ against eta and not seeing that... what did you see? Sounds like you spotted non identifiability,but maybe didn't know what it looked like?
What can I do to diagnose the problem?

My suggestions:
- always start simpler. Find a model that fits and then build up from there. If you jump to where things aren't working, the space of things that could have gone wrong is too large. 
- don't assume anything is right. I wouldn't buy that the whole model is specified correctly. I'd start there. How do you know the function value is right? Have you plugged in values and evaluated the lp__ coming out?
- were there divergences or problems with tree depth? If so, fix those first. 
- put more informative priors or more info / structure in the model. And think generatively while you're at it. When you put down priors, draw from them when you simulate data. 
- what does your posterior predictive check look like? If you simulate fake data and it looks just like the real data, that also signals a non identifiability. If the fake data looks nothing like real data, then something else is wrong.

I've attached a description of the model (stanusers.pdf), our current Stan code (pollen.stan), the Bash script we use to run it in cmdstan 2.12.0 (run4chains.sh) with a simulated data set (simdataBrostrom.txt), example trace plots (stansimTrace.pdf), and kernel density plots of the posterior distributions of each parameter, with the true values as red lines (plotpostparms.pdf). Pairs plots of the posterior distributions were too big too post here, but showed obvious problems with eta, and some fairly strong correlations among some other parameters.
I missed the other parameters. It sounds like you're describing a non identified model. Check lp__ first and see what you get.

For this case, the true values used to generate simulated data in R were:

    a <- c(0.10471002, -0.03106714)
    B <- matrix(c(-0.04184048, 0.06290105, 0.01222532, -0.03466200), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
    x0 <- c(-0.7, 0.9)
    Sigma <- matrix(c(0.01, -0.005, -0.005, 0.03), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
    eta <- c(-0.69, -0.40)

and we generated 1001 equally-spaced observations, each with n = 1000 in the multinomials.

Hope that helps.



Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
parts: Thank you. That was very helpful. We've established that it is an identifiability problem after all (obvious in retrospect). Traceplots of lp__ were indeed roughly the same for chains with very different values for eta. Once we knew where to look, it was easy to show that adding eta makes the model not identifiable (it was working fine before we added that). It's possible to show that for any set of parameters (a, B, x_0, Sigma, eta), there is another set (a + B * eta, B, x_0 - eta, Sigma, 0) with the same likelihood (and it's nothing to do with the nonlinear transformation, just a translation of the latent process).

parts:
Informative priors, I think. We can probably get fairly good prior information about eta. Also, we may be able to get prior information about x at some time points (at the end of the time series, not at the start), which will help. But also, a lot of what we're interested in is differences in x between time points, or derivatives of the expected value of x at time points, which are invariant under translation and so are not affected by the identifiability problem.

Matt

Jacobian warnings are a function of the Stan program and don't have anything to do with runtime diagnosis. 

Plotting lp__ against eta and not seeing that... what did you see? Sounds like you spotted non identifiability,but maybe didn't know what it looked like?


What can I do to diagnose the problem?

My suggestions:
- always start simpler. Find a model that fits and then build up from there. If you jump to where things aren't working, the space of things that could have gone wrong is too large. 
- don't assume anything is right. I wouldn't buy that the whole model is specified correctly. I'd start there. How do you know the function value is right? Have you plugged in values and evaluated the lp__ coming out?
- were there divergences or problems with tree depth? If so, fix those first. 
- put more informative priors or more info / structure in the model. And think generatively while you're at it. When you put down priors, draw from them when you simulate data. 
- what does your posterior predictive check look like? If you simulate fake data and it looks just like the real data, that also signals a non identifiability. If the fake data looks nothing like real data, then something else is wrong.
